analysis.one_liner: Requires a seven-day waiting period before most firearm transfers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote and died in the House Judiciary Committee at the end of the 118th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a federal crime, punishable by up to five years in prison or a fine, to transfer a firearm to an unlicensed buyer unless at least seven calendar days had passed since the buyer offered to take possession. It exempts temporary transfers at shooting ranges, hunting and pest-control uses, and transfers where the owner is present. It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: People at risk of impulsive gun violence — including those considering suicide or in moments of anger — gain the safety margin of a mandatory pause before a firearm changes hands. Communities affected by gun violence and law enforcement gain from fewer guns sold on the spot.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People at risk of impulsive gun violence

how_it_helps.text: Creates a seven-day waiting period between an offer to take possession of a firearm and the transfer itself, for transfers to unlicensed individuals [S2][S3].
Imposes criminal penalties of up to five years in prison or a fine of up to $250,000 on violations [S2][S3].

Exempts temporary transfers for target shooting, hunting, trapping, farm or ranch pest control, fishing, and transfers in the owner's presence, so routine recreational and farm uses are not delayed [S2][S3].
Takes effect 90 days after enactment, giving buyers and sellers time to adjust [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Firearm buyers who want a gun quickly — including people facing an urgent threat who might want same-day protection — bear a mandatory delay. Gun dealers and private sellers would face a week-long wait between sale and handover, and anyone who ignores the wait risks criminal prosecution.

drawbacks.text: The waiting period applies even to buyers with urgent need, such as a person facing a credible threat who wants a firearm quickly; the bill's exemptions cover recreation and farm use but not self-defense purchases [S3].
The penalty is criminal — up to five years in prison — for ordinary private sellers who misjudge the seven-day clock, a heavy consequence for non-commercial transactions [S3].

It applies only to transfers to unlicensed individuals, so transactions routed through licensed dealers follow existing law; a seller could structure a transfer as a temporary lending arrangement within one of the exemptions [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A waiting period is one of the modest, well-studied tools for reducing impulsive gun deaths, and the exemptions protect most recreational uses. The cost falls on the small share of buyers with urgent, legitimate needs, and the criminal penalty is steep for a rule that depends on private parties counting days correctly. On balance a defensible safety measure, though its narrow cosponsor base suggests it was written as a statement bill rather than negotiated legislation.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Elissa Slotkin introduced the Pause for Gun Safety Act on March 29, 2023, joined by two cosponsors [S1][S4].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S5].
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — occurred before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No policy changed, so gun sales continue with no waiting period for private transfers; sellers and buyers who prefer immediate handovers are unaffected, and the measure's backers gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Sellers and buyers of guns, unchanged

for.name: Rep. Elissa Slotkin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create a seven-day waiting period for firearm transfers.

for.name: Reps. Ann Kuster and David Trone
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; they were its only cosponsors.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over firearm policy
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 29, 2023 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had three Democratic backers and no Republican support in the record, and a Republican-run committee never acted on it.

industries.note: A waiting period delays the moment a sale becomes a completed transfer, cutting into quick, impulse-driven purchases. That delay is the safety benefit ordinary people would get from the bill, so the industry's convenience ran against it in this case — though the practical stakes for dealers were modest given the bill's exemptions and its death in committee.
